name: Uma Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and lead the cello section for a small opera company, record study passages and teach advanced pupils. I have a master’s in music and other players ask me to settle tricky entrances, but our short opera season pays less than comparable senior chairs. I love the moment the lower strings make a singer feel safe.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does that season work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner does part-time bakery shifts and our children are grown. We pay a mortgage and have only three weeks of expenses saved because the company has cut rehearsal weeks and I help with my mother’s bills. There are few comparable senior chairs nearby; I use AI every day to sort my own score notes, then check markings against the printed part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the opera players that a quicker schedule helps if the paid rehearsal and preparation hours are printed beside it. I would ask the company to sign that sheet before we learn a new act.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company already shortened rehearsal weeks, so a quiet AI plateau does not make my wages safe. Three weeks saved leaves little room when my mother’s bill and the mortgage arrive together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep paid opera and advanced pupils, ask for written rehearsal and preparation hours, and request an actual pension estimate. In the first plateau year I would compare the figure with our mortgage and my mother’s costs before setting any retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even without a new AI shock. I can lead the cellos through a hard entrance. I cannot bow a missing rehearsal wage into being.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the company cut already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It dropped one paid rehearsal week from the last production. I still had to prepare the score, so I asked for that time on the next contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the pension estimate change work this winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It is a number to check, not an income I can assume. I need paid opera and pupils while we look at it.

I would ask the company to **sign the schedule** before a new act.
think: A **cut rehearsal week** has already reduced my lower-paid senior wages despite the skill my cello section needs.
Our **three-week reserve** leaves mortgage and my mother’s bills exposed when opera work pauses.
do: Keep **paid opera and pupils** while requesting written rehearsal and preparation hours.
Request an **actual pension estimate** now and compare it with mortgage and family bills in the plateau year.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing wage gaps.
S0.quote: I cannot bow a missing rehearsal wage into being.
fieldNote: Her **senior skill** brings responsibility, while the short season pays below comparable chairs.
The **thin reserve** and existing rehearsal cut justify anxiety in a plateau.

steps.text: Keep paid opera and advanced pupils; request written rehearsal and preparation hours
Request actual pension estimate now; compare with mortgage and family bills in plateau year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our players that generated study tracks may be quick, but someone still has to hear a real bowing problem. I would ask the company which recorded guides and preparation hours remain paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Study passages and paid score preparation are about a quarter of my own income. I expect generated parts to displace some of that work, and three weeks saved cannot bridge a season-long loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would request written guide and preparation rates, then ask for a paid demonstration of a new score-comparison tool. In disruption’s first year I would test only my own nameless cello passage after approved local company storage, play the printed part against every suggested change, and stop at a wrong bowing or a file leaving the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real part of my wages shrinking. A machine can flag a note, but it cannot listen to the player whose hand is hurting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you upload a pupil’s lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Their names and recordings stay in our lesson folder. My own nameless passage is enough to test the tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if training is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the printed score until the company funds a paid lesson. I already give away enough preparation time.

I would say **real bowing problems** still need a player’s ear.
think: **Guides and preparation** make a quarter of my income.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot cover a long loss of that pay.
do: Request **written guide rates** and paid tool instruction next month.
Test the **score comparison** only after paid instruction and approved local storage on my nameless passage; play print, stop errors/leaks.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely lost guide and preparation income.
S1.quote: A machine can flag a note, but it cannot listen to the player whose hand is hurting.
fieldNote: The **new score tool** requires paid instruction, approved local storage, owned nameless music and manual bowing checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the cello section that thinking AGI in 2028 could make study passages before robots can play strings around 2031. I would ask for signed paid rehearsal dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect recorded study work and two preparation calls to disappear in 2028. That is close to a third of my already low senior pay, and I have caught myself awake adding the mortgage figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would total the study and preparation invoices and get the next opera weeks in writing. In the first year after 2028, if those fees end, I would apply only for a posted paid conservatory ensemble tutor role that accepts my music master’s and cello-section leadership, pays for human rehearsals and individual correction, and offers written net pay after travel replacing the lost wages with a train home; I would keep opera and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by an expected third of my own wages disappearing before another senior chair opens. I can apply, but there are few local places to apply to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the ensemble tutor still do in person?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would hear a young cellist lock an arm and change the bowing in the room. A posted school must actually pay for that human correction, not just for a title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When do robots enter this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card puts hands-on string players around 2031, three years after thinking AGI. My recording buyer can leave in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the opera company that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to negotiate paid preparation before score software sets the rate. Robot string players around 2034 do not settle tonight’s rehearsal bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the study passages to thin over those years, and our little reserve makes waiting expensive. I would rather bargain for a paid term with the musicians than pay for a new certificate nobody asked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would bring our signed preparation invoices to the musicians association and ask the opera company for a two-year written teaching and rehearsal schedule with paid score preparation. In the first year after 2031 I would keep the cello section and advanced pupils only on paid hours, and if the company cuts both study and rehearsal fees I would seek a posted paid conservatory cello-tutor vacancy accepting my master’s and section leadership, paying for live rehearsals and individual correction, with written net pay after travel replacing both lost fees and a train home; I would not leave current paid work before a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about pay sliding while we can see it coming. A signed preparation hour is more useful than another speech about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the association guarantee a contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would ask colleagues to bring their invoices and make a written request together. The company still has to sign and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the conservatory has no real opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep every paid opera and pupil call and check the next actual posting. My degree cannot create a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger players that a decade until AGI by 2036 is long enough to get written use and rehearsal terms into the contract. Robot strings around 2039 do not pay our mortgage today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might play fewer evenings, but I cannot count a pension amount I have never seen. The short season and my mother’s bills still leave less than a month saved, even before recordings change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension estimate and a written two-year opera schedule, then put ten percent of each extra paid recital fee after mortgage, food, travel and my mother’s bill toward two months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid opera and pupils while the calls last, and seek a posted paid ensemble-tutor role only if both study and rehearsal fees have fallen, the employer accepts my master’s and cello-section leadership, paid live coaching and correction hours remain, written net pay after travel replaces both losses and the last train works; I would stay in paid music until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the thin household cushion even with ten years to see recordings change. A long forecast is not a paid rehearsal week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra recital pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then nothing new goes into the reserve from recitals. Two months is a goal, not money we already hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would put the actual estimate beside our bills and health first. I have no date fixed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because study and preparation fees could take a third of my already short season. Written paid opera weeks, a real conservatory tutor posting accepting my master’s and a net offer after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the section leader to mark a new cello score before rehearsal. Bowings on a cello score may look like pencil marks, but they are paid hours of my life.

headlineQuote: Bowings on a cello score may look like pencil marks, but they are paid hours of my life.
portrait: Uma is a **senior cello leader** with a music master’s, opera work, study recordings and advanced pupils.
Her **short season**, low senior pay, three-week reserve, mortgage and family support make her finances tight.
She uses **AI daily** for notes but tests a new score tool only with paid instruction, approved storage and manual playing.
She seeks **paid preparation terms** collectively and a qualifying posted human tutor role if fees fall.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could erase study and preparation fees worth nearly a third of her own pay.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **written paid opera weeks**, a posted tutor vacancy accepting her master’s and written replacement net after travel.
